title: ArrayDeque replaces Stack — push/pop/peek LIFO behavior
shortTitle: ArrayDeque replaces Stack — push/pop/peek LIFO behavior

s1_definition.profdef: `ArrayDeque` is the recommended replacement for the legacy `Stack` class. Stack extends Vector (every method synchronized — slow even for single-threaded use) and exposes `get(index)` which violates LIFO abstraction. ArrayDeque implements `Deque` — `push(e)` adds to head, `pop()` removes from head, `peek()` views head without removing — all O(1) amortized, no synchronization overhead. ArrayDeque is backed by a resizable circular array — contiguous memory = cache-friendly = faster than LinkedList as a stack/queue.
s1_definition.analogy: **Stack (legacy)** = an old safe with a heavy lock that opens/closes for EVERY operation (synchronized) — even when only one person uses it. Plus, the safe has a side window letting you grab items from the middle (get by index) — not how a stack should work! **ArrayDeque** = a modern spring-loaded tray: put on top (push), take from top (pop), peek at top. No lock (fast), no side window (proper LIFO), backed by an efficient circular array.
s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayDeque = fast LIFO stack: push/pop/peek. No synchronization overhead (unlike Stack). No random access (proper stack abstraction). Use Deque interface, not Stack class.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ArrayDeque` is the recommended replacement for the legacy `Stack` class. Stack extends Vector (every method synchronized — slow even for single-threaded use) and exposes `get(index)` which violates LIFO abstraction. ArrayDeque implements `Deque` — `push(e)` adds to head, `pop()` removes from head, `peek()` views head without removing — all O(1) amortized, no synchronization overhead. ArrayDeque is backed by a resizable circular array — contiguous memory = cache-friendly = faster than LinkedList as a stack/queue.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **Stack (legacy)** = an old safe with a heavy lock that opens/closes for EVERY operation (synchronized) — even when only one person uses it. Plus, the safe has a side window letting you grab items from the middle (get by index) — not how a stack should work! **ArrayDeque** = a modern spring-loaded tray: put on top (push), take from top (pop), peek at top. No lock (fast), no side window (proper LIFO), backed by an efficient circular array.

**One line to remember:** ArrayDeque = fast LIFO stack: push/pop/peek. No synchronization overhead (unlike Stack). No random access (proper stack abstraction). Use Deque interface, not Stack class.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto ArrayDeque replacing the legacy Stack. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how ArrayDeque replacing the legacy Stack solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is an `ArrayDeque` used as a LIFO stack to track Rajesh's recent transaction amounts for an undo feature.

**Step 1.** Each new transaction amount is added with `push()`, placing it at the head so the most recent one is always on top.

**Step 2.** An undo request calls `pop()`, which removes and returns the top amount, reversing the latest transaction first.

**Step 3.** A `peek()` reads the current top without removing it, so the system can show the next item to undo while the deque keeps strict last-in-first-out order.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ArrayDeque as STACK (LIFO) ═══

  push("A"): [A]              ← top
  push("B"): [B][A]           ← top is B
  push("C"): [C][B][A]        ← top is C
  pop():     returns C → [B][A]
  pop():     returns B → [A]
  peek():    returns A (not removed)

  ═══ WHY NOT Stack class ═══
  Stack: synchronized (slow) + get(index) (violates LIFO) + extends Vector (legacy)
  ArrayDeque: no sync (fast) + no random access (proper LIFO) + circular array (cache-friendly)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
     Banking Transaction Undo / Call Stack
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Operation Processor                      │
  │  push(op) → execute → undo via pop()      │
  └────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘
                       │ LIFO
                       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Deque<Op> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()     │
  │  (fast, unsynchronized, cache-friendly)   │
  │  NOT legacy Stack (synchronized, Vector)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayDeque is the modern replacement for the legacy Stack class. Stack extends Vector — every method synchronized (unnecessary overhead in single-threaded code) and exposes `get(index)` which violates the LIFO abstraction. ArrayDeque implements Deque — `push()`/`pop()`/`peek()` provide proper LIFO behavior, backed by a circular array (cache-friendly, no per-node allocation like LinkedList). The Java documentation explicitly states: "This class is likely to be faster than Stack when used as a stack." Always use `Deque<String> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()`, never `Stack<String> stack = new Stack<>()`.
